questions.stem: Your hybrid project is delivering remote monitoring for a water company's 140 pumping stations: the field hardware is installed to a fixed plan and the monitoring software is built in sprints. Go-live is in six weeks, and the design includes remote access for the hardware vendor's engineers. The national cyber security agency has just raised the threat level for the water sector after attacks on remote-access tools at two utilities abroad. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the water company's security team to review the vendor remote-access design against the agency's new advisory before go-live.
options.rationale: The design was approved against the old threat picture. The organisation's security function owns the judgement of what the new level requires, and asking now leaves six weeks to act on the answer.

options.text: Tell the steering group now that the advisory may change the access design and the go-live date, and record it in the risk register.
options.rationale: A possible change to design and date is something governance should hear about before it is certain, not after. Making it visible now lets the sponsor prepare instead of being surprised at go-live.

options.text: Remove vendor remote access from scope, with the vendor's engineers attending stations in person for all support until the threat level falls again.
options.rationale: This may be where the review ends up, but it decides a security question without the security function and commits to site visits across 140 stations. The candidate reaches for the most drastic response before the threat has been assessed.

options.text: Proceed to go-live as planned, because the remote-access design passed independent penetration testing last month and nothing in the project itself has changed.
options.rationale: The project has not changed, but the environment it will operate in has. A test passed against last month's threat picture does not show that the design is adequate for this month's.

options.text: Ask the hardware vendor to confirm in writing that its remote-access tool is not the one attacked abroad, and proceed with go-live once it has.
options.rationale: A reasonable question to ask, but a raised threat level concerns the class of attack, not one product, and the vendor is not neutral on whether its own access route is safe. The candidate narrows a sector-wide warning to a single supplier assurance.

questions.explanation: A change in the external threat environment can make a design that was adequate yesterday inadequate today, even though nothing inside the project has changed. The response is to have the function that owns the risk reassess the design against the new conditions and to tell governance early that scope or dates may move, rather than either proceeding on old assurance or deciding the remedy alone.
questions.mindset: Re-test past approvals when the world they were made in changes.

questions.stem: You manage the build of a new research laboratory for a university. Match each external development to the party who owns the first response to it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The government announces an enhanced tax credit for capital spending on research facilities, which the university might claim if costs are recorded in a particular way from now on.
A revised national standard for laboratory fume extraction is published; it applies to designs submitted for building approval after June, and your detailed design goes in for approval in July.
The country where your fume cupboards are made sharply raises its export duty on them; the supply contract is on delivered duty paid terms.

options.text: The university's finance and tax function
options.rationale: Whether the university can and should claim a tax credit is a tax judgement for the organisation, not the project. The project's part is to change how it records costs once finance says what is needed.

options.text: The lead designer responsible for the building services design
options.rationale: A standard that will apply at submission is a design requirement, and assessing what it changes is the designer's professional responsibility. Cost and time effects then follow through the project's normal change process.

options.text: The fume cupboard supplier, under its contract
options.rationale: Delivered duty paid terms put export and import duties on the seller. The rise is the supplier's cost to absorb, and the project's role is to hold the contract rather than to solve it.

options.text: The project board, as a change to the approved scope
options.rationale: Not used. None of these developments is yet a scope change: each first needs assessment or action by the party that holds the relevant expertise or obligation. The board may later receive consequences, but routing every external change to it first skips the owner.

questions.explanation: External developments arrive at the project, but the first response to each belongs to whoever holds the relevant expertise or contractual obligation: tax questions to the tax function, requirements to the designer, cost risks to the party the contract assigns them to. The project manager's job is to route each one to its owner and then integrate the consequences, not to absorb them all as project decisions.
questions.mindset: Ask who already owns an external change before deciding how the project absorbs it.

questions.stem: Your organisation is building a container terminal under a contract with a force majeure clause, a change-in-law clause, a price adjustment clause and a liquidated damages clause. Complete each sentence with the clause the contractor would rely on. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: After the contract was signed, a new national regulation required every crane to carry an extra anti-collision system. The contractor's claim for the added cost is made under the
A volcanic eruption closed the region's airspace for nine days, so specialist commissioning staff could not reach site. The contractor's claim for extra time without penalty is made under the

options.text: change-in-law clause
options.rationale: A legal requirement introduced after signature could not have been priced at tender. The change-in-law clause exists to move that cost to the employer, because it is a change in the rules rather than in the market.

options.text: force majeure clause
options.rationale: An eruption is an event outside either party's control that neither could reasonably have prevented. Force majeure typically relieves the affected party of delay penalties for that period, usually as time rather than money.

options.text: price adjustment clause
options.rationale: Not used. Price adjustment covers movement in market prices against an index. A new legal requirement adds work rather than changing the price of existing work, so treating it as indexation misclassifies the event.

options.text: liquidated damages clause
options.rationale: Not used. Liquidated damages are what the employer recovers for the contractor's delay, so the contractor never relies on this clause to claim. The other clauses decide whether those damages apply at all.

questions.explanation: Contracts sort external events by kind: a change in the law after signature, an event beyond either party's control, and a movement in market prices each have their own mechanism and remedy, often money for the first and time for the second. Classifying the event correctly comes first, because it decides which clause applies and what relief is available.
questions.mindset: Classify the external event before reaching for a remedy, because the contract sorts them by kind.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is replacing a distribution warehouse, with its stock-control software built in sprints. Demolition will send 4,000 tonnes of mixed waste to landfill: 1,500 tonnes before 1 April and 2,500 tonnes after. Landfill costs a £35.00 per tonne gate fee plus landfill tax, which rises from £103.70 to £126.15 per tonne on 1 April. A recycling contractor can take 60% of the post-April tonnage for £58.00 per tonne, plus a one-off £12,000 set-up charge. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Extra landfill tax caused by the rise if nothing changes, in £
blanks.rationale: Only the 2,500 tonnes after 1 April are affected. The rise is 126.15 − 103.70 = £22.45 per tonne, and 2,500 × 22.45 = £56,125.

blanks.label: Net saving from sending 60% of the post-April waste to the recycling contractor, in £
blanks.rationale: Diverted tonnage is 60% of 2,500 = 1,500 tonnes. Landfill would cost 1,500 × (126.15 + 35.00) = £241,725. Recycling costs 1,500 × 58.00 + 12,000 = £99,000. The net saving is 241,725 − 99,000 = £142,725.

questions.explanation: An external tax change should be costed on the quantities it actually touches, which here is only the work falling after its effective date, and then used to re-test options that were not worth it under the old rate. A rise in the cost of one route often turns an alternative from marginal to clearly better, and the comparison must include every cost on both sides, including one-off charges and fees that do not change.
questions.mindset: When the outside world reprices one option, re-run the comparison with all the others.

questions.stem: Your agile team ships releases of a pharmacy dispensing system on fixed dates. A national rule takes effect on 1 November: systems must reject electronic prescriptions that lack a new verification code. The health ministry requires each supplier's change to have been live in every pharmacy for at least six weeks before that date. Select the latest release that meets the ministry's requirement.

graphic.title: Release timeline for the dispensing system, with the rule's effective date of 1 November
graphic.caption: Select a release. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between releases, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Release 14 — live in all pharmacies 3 June
regions.rationale: Release 14 meets the requirement with five months to spare, but it is not the latest that does. Pulling the change into June displaces work already planned for that release without any regulatory need.

regions.label: Release 15 — live in all pharmacies 1 September
regions.rationale: Six weeks before 1 November is 20 September. Release 15 is live on 1 September, about eight and a half weeks before the rule takes effect, and it is the last release that clears the six-week requirement.

regions.label: Release 16 — live in all pharmacies 22 September
regions.rationale: Release 16 is live before the rule takes effect, which is what makes it tempting, but only five weeks and five days before. The candidate has checked the effective date and not the ministry's six-week live-running condition.

regions.label: Release 17 — live in all pharmacies 3 November
regions.rationale: This arrives after the rule is already in force, so pharmacies would be running a non-compliant system for two days and the six-week condition would not be met at all.

regions.label: Emergency patch channel — any date, for urgent defect fixes only
regions.rationale: The patch channel is reserved for urgent defects. Using it for a known, dated regulatory change misuses an exception route and still has to satisfy the six-week condition, which planning into a release already does.

questions.explanation: A regulatory deadline is often not the date the rule takes effect but an earlier date implied by conditions attached to it, such as a period of live running or certification. Work back from the effective date through every condition to find the true deadline, then plan the change into the last regular release that meets it, so it neither misses the rule nor displaces other work early.
questions.mindset: Find the real deadline by working back through every condition attached to the rule.
